message.content:
The Greyhound coughed me onto the curb of Havenwood, spitting me out with a shudder and a plume of exhaust. It wasn't a glamorous arrival, but then again, neither was I. Dust clung to my jeans and the city had left a permanent grit under my fingernails, a stark contrast to the sleepy charm of the town I’d left behind a decade ago. A familiar figure, taller than I remembered, waved from across the street. Liam. 

“Mina! You made it!” He practically bounded towards me, his grin wide and genuine. It was a greeting that instantly eased the knot of anxiety I’d been carrying around since booking the ticket. He smelled of sawdust and something faintly sweet, probably coffee. "Let’s get this show on the road, huh? We've got a mountain of boxes to wrestle into place.”

The “show” was “The Daily Grind,” Liam’s dream, a cafe he’d been planning for years. It occupied the old Miller’s Hardware building, a sprawling space with exposed brick and high ceilings that needed a serious dose of cozy. Right now, that meant unpacking. A delivery of mismatched tables and chairs sat stacked haphazardly on the sidewalk, alongside boxes overflowing with linens, mugs, and the essential paraphernalia of a coffee shop. Liam, ever the organizer, had already laid out a system. "Okay, tables to the back, chairs near the windows, linens and mugs – those go into the storage room. I’ve labelled everything.”

We began methodically, a silent choreography of lifting, shifting, and placing. I wrestled a particularly stubborn oak table, its legs resisting my efforts until Liam stepped in, effortlessly maneuvering it into position. "These old things," he chuckled, wiping his brow. "They have a mind of their own.” A quick check of the schedule revealed a small wrinkle. Mrs. Hawthorne, the local baker who was supplying the pastries, had called to say she was running late. “She got held up with a wedding cake order,” Liam explained, “Says she’ll be here by noon, though. We were hoping to have a sample spread out for the painters when they arrive."

"No problem," I said, feeling surprisingly at home already. "We’ll hold off on the display until then. More time to get these tables set up." We paused, both needing a moment to catch our breath. Liam produced a thermos of iced coffee and a plate of slightly-squished cookies from a cooler. “Fuel for the workers,” he announced with a grin. The coffee was strong and sweet, the cookies crumbly and comforting, a perfect taste of Havenwood. 

Refreshed, we returned to the task at hand. I was layering a cheerful floral pattern on one of the tables, while Liam began arranging the chairs around it. He was humming a tuneless melody, a habit from childhood that I remembered vividly. We worked in comfortable silence, the rhythmic clatter of chairs and the rustle of linens filling the space, slowly transforming the empty shell of a building into something warm and inviting.
